claims.text: Spin-polarized density functional theory can be used to detect ferromagnetic ground states.
Ferromagnetic ground states can be identified by comparing the total energies of different magnetic configurations.
The relevant comparison includes ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and non-magnetic computational states.
GGA or LDA exchange-correlation functionals can capture magnetic interactions in suitable systems.
Crystal-lattice geometry controls electronic overlaps relevant to magnetic ordering.
Crystal-lattice geometry mediates exchange interactions relevant to magnetic ordering.
DFT energy comparisons identify which modeled magnetic configuration has the lowest total energy.
A ferromagnetic configuration having the lowest calculated energy indicates that exchange interactions favor parallel spin alignment.
Exchange interactions that favor parallel spin alignment stabilize a ferromagnetic ground state.
The calculations will show that the ferromagnetic state has lower energy than the modeled alternative states.
The lower-energy ferromagnetic solution will have a finite and robust magnetic moment per magnetic atom.
Non-magnetic and antiferromagnetic solutions can serve as computational baselines.
Standard DFT is most applicable for this purpose when it adequately captures electron-correlation effects.
Strongly correlated materials or materials with complex magnetic interactions may require methods beyond standard DFT.
Calculated magnetic energy differences and magnetic moments are sensitive to the exchange-correlation functional and other computational parameters.
Experimental verification is necessary for definitive proof of a ferromagnetic ground state.

contradictions.description: The initial state is only a generic candidate with potential magnetic ordering, but the predicted outcome unconditionally states that the ferromagnetic state will be lowest in energy.

The mechanism presents DFT as a comparison that may identify any configuration as lowest in energy, whereas the falsification rule treats a non-ferromagnetic lowest-energy result as falsifying the method's reliability rather than as a valid finding that the tested material is not ferromagnetic within the model.
